query: If films addressed the most common audience complaints, how much would positive sentiment increase?

per_column.name: writing_quality_issue
per_column.rationale: Encodes the specific audience complaint (weak script, predictable story, poor dialogue). The query targets 'addressing the most common audience complaints', so this is the intervenable lever a filmmaker could actually change/fix. It is clearly implied by the query.

per_column.name: complaint_multiplicity
per_column.rationale: A boolean flag for whether multiple complaints co-occur. This is still part of the complaint-structure being intervened on rather than an independent common cause; it is directly implied by the query's reference to complaints. Not a common cause of both treatment and outcome.

per_column.name: counterbalancing_positive_elements
per_column.rationale: Positive elements (strong cast, good visuals, emotional resonance) and the presence of complaints both feed into the overall sentiment/rating; conditioning on the outcome-adjacent positives resembles a collider/mediator on the outcome side rather than a common cause of the complaint and the sentiment. It does not adjust confounding.

judge.rationale: A genuine, intervenable treatment is present: the writing-quality complaint is something filmmakers could actually address/fix, satisfying part (a) of the technical claim. However, part (b) fails entirely: none of the added columns are confounders — common causes of both the complaint and the sentiment that must be adjusted before reading off a counterfactual (e.g., genre, budget, director reputation, reviewer disposition, marketing/expectations). 'counterbalancing_positive_elements' sits on the outcome side (collider/mediator), not as a backdoor confounder. Because no confounders are supplied, no unnamed confounders demonstrate the interventional capability, so the columns do not realise the what-if claim despite having a valid treatment.
